articles.title: Korean Peninsula pacemaker — Is South Korea Helping or Hurting US Alliance? - The Korea Daily
articles.summary: Korean Peninsula pacemaker — Is South Korea Helping or Hurting US Alliance?  The Korea Daily
articles.full_text:
During last month’s 81st United Nations General Assembly, President Lee Jae-myung re-emphasized South Korea’s role as a Korean Peninsula pacemaker for peace. This follows his promise during last year’s first summit with U.S. President Donald Trump, where he asked Trump to be the ‘peacemaker’ while positioning himself as the pacemaker assisting him. However, looking at the recent actions of the South Korean government, there is growing concern that rather than becoming a pacemaker, it might turn into a ‘troublemaker’ causing confusion in the ROK-U.S. alliance and peace on the Korean Peninsula.
While covering the Aspen Security Forum last July, I had a conversation with a 25-year veteran foreign policy and security reporter who posed this question: ‘Wasn’t there a uniquely low level of mention regarding North Korea this year compared to last year?’
Looking back, that was indeed the case. While North Korea did appear when adversaries of the U.S. were discussed alongside China, Russia, and Iran, discussions dealing intensively with the direct threat of North Korea decreased noticeably. This contrasted sharply with last year, when North Korea’s cyber threats and other issues were treated as major agenda items. Even though North Korea continues to build its nuclear and missile capabilities and strengthen military cooperation with Russia, its presence in U.S. foreign policy discourse is fading.
Precisely because of this, the South Korean government must take action. It needs to inject agendas and capture attention within the U.S. Congress, executive branch, think tanks, and academia so that the North Korean nuclear issue, cyber threats, and human rights issues continue to be discussed. This is public diplomacy as well. Public diplomacy is not merely about promoting K-pop and K-food.
In particular, North Korean human rights are a crucial diplomatic leverage point that South Korea can utilize. In the U.S., North Korean human rights is treated as a bipartisan issue, as evidenced last June when Democratic Senator Tim Kimb and Republican Senator Dan Sullivan jointly sponsored a bill to reauthorize the North Korean Human Rights Act. Furthermore, U.S. law mandates a special envoy on North Korean human rights to raise international awareness of the severity of the situation. In the past, South Korea’s progressive administrations were criticized for placing North Korean human rights on the back burner in inter-Korean relations, and the current government is facing similar concerns. Even while pursuing dialogue with North Korea, the human rights issue of North Korean citizens must not be pushed to the margins of negotiations.
An even bigger problem is that at a time when North Korea-related agendas should be elevated in the U.S., diplomacy with Washington repeatedly displays scenes that amplify confusion rather than build trust. Recent discussions on U.S.-Korea investments are a prime example. When President Trump successively announced an $8.4 billion oil recovery project and an Alaska LNG investment, the South Korean government drew a line, stating the details were not agreed upon or required further review. The pattern of the U.S. president making announcements as if matters were finalized, only for the South Korean government to issue corrections, has repeated itself.
With this style of diplomacy toward the U.S., it is difficult for President Lee’s desired ‘pacemaker’ role to gain traction. Coordinating the pace between Washington and Pyongyang requires, above all, the trust of President Trump and Washington. If differing messages are sent even on trade and investment issues, how much would the U.S. trust South Korea if it claims to take on a mediating role in the much more sensitive North Korean nuclear negotiations? What a pacemaker needs is not a mere declaration, but diplomatic credibility that the counterpart can trust and rely upon.
The case of the past Moon Jae-in administration can serve as a counter-example. Back when inter-Korean and North Korea-U.S. summit diplomacy unfolded in 2018, former President Moon gained attention as a mediator. However, around the time of the 2019 Hanoi North Korea-U.S. summit, discontent arose in Washington over rushing the easing of sanctions. Furthermore, Pyongyang communicated directly with Trump, losing the need to go through South Korea. Having styled itself as a mediator, the very space for mediation vanished.
If President Lee genuinely wants to become a pacemaker for peace on the Korean Peninsula, he must straighten out the sequence. He must elevate the presence of the North Korean issue in the U.S., establish clear principles on the North Korean nuclear issue and human rights, and firmly solidify trust between South Korea and the United States first.
A pacemaker is not a position acquired simply by making a self-declaration. It is a role assumed only when the accompanying partner trusts you enough to entrust you with the pace. The pacemaker intended to lead peace on the Korean Peninsula must never become a troublemaker that tangles the flow.

articles.title: Chip industry activists call for South Korea to recognise cancer cases - RTL Today
articles.summary: Chip industry activists call for South Korea to recognise cancer cases  RTL Today
articles.full_text:
South Korean activists campaigning for workplace safety in the nation's booming semiconductor industry called on the government on Wednesday to recognise the cancer diagnoses of three former SK hynix employees as work-related illnesses.
SK hynix, along with fellow South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics, has emerged as a key player in the booming artificial intelligence industry, with its cutting-edge memory chips crucial to powering the sector's rapid growth.
Establishing direct links between semiconductor work and certain cancers can be contentious, with research inconclusive. But fabrication and assembly plant workers can face exposure to solvents, acids, toxic metals and chemical gases, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Samsung issued a public apology in 2018 to workers -- many of them young women -- who had developed cancer after working at some of its factories, paying out 150 million won per case (about $130,000 at the time) after a decade-long dispute.
Supporters for the Health and Rights of People in the Semiconductor Industry (SHARPS) , one of the groups that had pressured Samsung, said on Wednesday chemicals classified as carcinogens were being used by SK hynix.
"We have confirmed that several substances on SK hynix's own list of prohibited chemicals are in fact being used, including nickel and its compounds," Lee Sang-soo, a SHARPS activist, told a news conference, citing data reported by SK hynix to the environment ministry.
SK hynix said in a statement sent to AFP it was "taking various measures to more objectively identify the characteristics of disease occurrence" and was fully cooperating with government inquiries.
The company, which did not address the specific claims, said it had taken "proactive industrial health measures including the development of a comprehensive support and compensation plan".
The husband of a former SK hynix worker who died from breast cancer called on the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service to recognise his wife's illness as work-related.
"I believe the nature of her job meant that she was inevitably exposed to various hazardous substances," Kim Yong-il, the husband of Yoon Young-mi, told the briefing outside the offices of the service, which is a government agency.
Yoon began working at SK hynix's Icheon chip plant in 1996 and was diagnosed with cancer in 2018. She died in April.
"The company and the relevant authorities must protect workers' right to health when it comes to occupational diseases in the semiconductor industry," Kim said.
Agency representative Ko Seong-yong of the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service told AFP that authorities would "process their cases as fast as possible".
"An epidemiological investigation is necessary. While it is difficult to give an exact timeframe, it could take around a year before a decision is made," he said.

articles.summary: Nara Space validates SK hynix chips in orbit after Nuri launch in South Korea - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
E3T Unit 2, a space verification satellite developed by Nara Space Technology (Nara Space), succeeded in two-way communication with the ground station after the fifth launch of Nuri. The satellite will verify in the actual space environment the performance of devices and parts developed in Korea, including SK hynix memory semiconductors onboard.
Nara Space said on the 8th that E3T Unit 2 was launched aboard Nuri at 12:25 p.m. on the 7th from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, South Jeolla, and communicated normally with the ground station.
E3T Unit 2 separated from Nuri about 17 minutes after liftoff and succeeded in its first two-way communication with the Nara Space satellite control center about 1 hour and 57 minutes later. It is currently conducting initial operations to check the satellite's basic status and key functions.
E3T Unit 2 is a 12U (1U is 10 cm in width, length, and height) class cubesat designed to test domestically developed semiconductors, electronic devices, and satellite parts in the actual space environment. It weighs about 18 kg, and Nara Space handled development of the satellite platform bus and post-launch operations.
The satellite carries SK hynix memory semiconductors, Inserasolution's high-speed precision steering mirror, Momentum Space's reaction wheel, and KAIST's attitude determination and system module. Cosmovy's hollow cathode for electric thrusters and Intergravity Technologies' avionics for an orbital transfer vehicle will also have their performance tested in space.
After completing initial orbital operations, E3T Unit 2 will begin full-scale verification missions. It will repeatedly operate the payloads, downlink data to the ground, and check how space radiation and large temperature swings affect the operation of devices and parts.
The satellite was developed under the Korea AeroSpace Administration's "domestically made device and part space verification support project." The Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) is in charge of program management and satellite system integration, and Nara Space handled the platform development and operations for Unit 2 following E3T Unit 1, which flew on the fourth Nuri launch last year.
Since its launch in Nov. last year, E3T Unit 1 has been carrying out missions to verify in the space environment domestically made devices and parts such as Samsung Electronics memory semiconductors and KAIST integrated circuits.
Park Jae-pil, CEO of Nara Space, said, "We will continue to keep pace with the global new space trend to expand verification opportunities for various space-grade devices and parts, and steadily build related capabilities so we can serve as a foundation for the growth of the domestic space device and parts industry."

articles.title: ​Applied Materials, Intel Partner on Next-Generation Chip Manufacturing Technology - www.thelec.net
articles.summary: ​Applied Materials, Intel Partner on Next-Generation Chip Manufacturing Technology  www.thelec.net
articles.full_text:
Applied Materials is partnering with Intel to develop next-generation semiconductor manufacturing technologies.
Applied Materials stated on October 6 that Intel has joined the Applied EPIC Center as a founding partner. The two companies will jointly research and develop process technologies and equipment across the front-end-of-line (FEOL), back-end-of-line (BEOL), and packaging stages of semiconductor manufacturing.
The collaboration is aimed at supporting higher interconnect density, improved power delivery, and enhanced thermal performance for high-performance computing (HPC) platforms. HPC platforms refer to integrated computing systems designed to support workloads suited to agentic artificial intelligence (AI).
The EPIC Center is a joint research and development facility for equipment and process innovation and commercialization being established in Silicon Valley. It aims to shorten the time required to commercialize semiconductor technologies, from the research stage to mass production.
Specifically, the companies will collaborate on new materials for next-generation logic processes, device architectures, and advanced interconnect processes, as well as Foveros-based 3D-stacking packaging processes. Applied Materials will provide Intel with a dedicated secure space inside the EPIC Center. Intel will connect infrastructure at its research and development campus in Hillsboro, Oregon, with the EPIC Center.
Gary Dickerson, chairman and chief executive officer (CEO) of Applied Materials, said, “Applied Materials and Intel have worked closely together for decades, pushing the boundaries of materials engineering to advance semiconductor technology.” He added, “With our teams working together at the EPIC Center, we will accelerate innovations in devices, interconnects, and packaging that will shape the future of AI computing.”
Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO, said, “Intel is working closely with partners across the ecosystem to drive innovation in performance, power efficiency, and packaging as demand for AI computing grows.” He added, “We look forward to expanding our collaboration at the Applied EPIC Center and accelerating the path from research in the US to high-volume manufacturing.”
The EPIC Center has more than 10 participating companies and organizations, including Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Micron Technology, TSMC, and Broadcom. The facility is in the final stages of preparations for operations. Its opening ceremony is scheduled for October 12. A total investment of 7 trillion won will be made in stages.

Summary
- Lisa Su said close cooperation with Korean partners including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is a core goal, and signaled long-term partnerships with them.
- Su said AMD is exploring cooperation opportunities across memory and foundry operations, including HBM4, and is urging a ramp-up in HBM4 production.
- Su said AMD will establish an AI research center in Korea within the year and hire hundreds of AI researchers to support the countrys AI ecosystem.

Lisa Su, chief executive officer of AMD, said working closely with Korean partners including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is a core priority for the company. She also indicated a willingness to build long-term partnerships with Korean semiconductor makers.
Su spoke to reporters after the "AMD Gamer Day" event at Seoul Dragon City in Yongsan on October 7, saying she returned to Korea because the countrys ecosystem is critically important for both supply and partnerships. With supply chains now highly complex, it is essential to make plans with partners on a three- to five-year horizon. It was Sus first visit to South Korea in seven months.
She likened cooperation in the semiconductor industry to a team sport, saying stronger collaboration with partners helps AMD better meet end-user demand. Su also underscored the need to work with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. She said she met with executives from both companies and is continuing to explore opportunities with Samsung across memory and foundry operations. On sixth-generation high-bandwidth memory, or HBM4, supplied to AMD by the two companies, Su said AMD is very satisfied and is urging a ramp-up in volume production.
Earlier on October 7, Su attended a meeting with Korean AI companies hosted by the Ministry of Science and ICT at the Four Seasons Hotel Seoul. The event followed a memorandum of understanding signed by the ministry and AMD in July. Su said AMD will establish an artificial intelligence research center in Korea within the year and hire hundreds of AI researchers. The move is aimed at advancing cutting-edge AI technology while supporting Koreas AI ecosystem.
At the meeting, participants discussed building heterogeneous computing infrastructure that combines AMD central processing units and graphics processing units with Korean neural processing units. They also discussed developing it into a reference model for use in global markets. Another topic was how Korean companies could participate in the ecosystem for ROCm, AMDs open-source AI software platform.

articles.title: Global banks lift S Korea's growth forecast on semiconductor boom - Asianet Newsable
articles.summary: Global banks lift S Korea's growth forecast on semiconductor boom  Asianet Newsable
articles.full_text:
Driven by a semiconductor export boom, major global investment banks have upgraded South Korea's economic growth forecast for this year to an average of 3.5%. The outlook for 2027 was also raised, bringing it closer to the Bank of Korea's projection.
Global investment banks revised up their forecasts for South Korea's economic growth this year and next, as a semiconductor export boom strengthens the outlook, according to The Korea Herald. Eight major global investment banks projected average growth of 3.5 per cent for this year at the end of September, up from 3.3 per cent a month earlier, according to figures released Wednesday by the Korea Center for International Finance, The Korea Herald reported.
Major Banks Raise Projections
JPMorgan raised its estimate to 4 per cent from 3.8 per cent, the highest among the eight banks. UBS lifted its forecast to 3.5 per cent from 2.8 per cent, while Bank of America increased its projection to 3.6 per cent from 3.1 per cent. Citi raised its estimate to 3.8 per cent from 3.7 per cent.
Outlook for 2027 Also Improves
Six of the eight banks also upgraded their forecasts for 2027, pushing the average to 2.8 per cent from 2.5 per cent at the end of August. That brought their outlook closer to the Bank of Korea's projection of 2.9 per cent.
Upward Trend Driven by Strong Performance
The revisions extend a run of upgrades that accelerated over the summer as chip exports surged and economic growth exceeded expectations. The banks' average forecast for this year has risen for six consecutive months, climbing from 2.4 per cent in April to 3 per cent in June and 3.2 per cent in July. By July, six of the eight banks expected growth of at least 3 per cent, double the number a month earlier.
Real gross domestic product expanded 1.8 per cent in the first quarter from the previous quarter and another 0.6 per cent in the second. The second-quarter gain exceeded the central bank's May projection of 0.2 per cent, strengthening the case for higher annual forecasts.
Semiconductor Boom and Record Exports
Exports reached a monthly record of USD 120.94 billion in September, up 83.5 per cent from a year earlier. Semiconductor shipments topped USD 60 billion for the first time, accounting for roughly half the total, while the trade surplus hit a record USD 49.85 billion.
Broader Consensus on Growth
The upgrades put the banks' average above the Bank of Korea's forecast of 3.3 per cent, raised in August. The central bank also lifted its projection for next year to 2.9 per cent from 2.1 per cent.
Other international institutions have also raised their forecasts. The Asian Development Bank lifted its projection for this year to 3.2 per cent in September, up 0.6 percentage point from July. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development raised its estimate to 3.7 per cent, up 1.1 percentage points from June, the largest upward revision among G20 economies.

articles.title: AMD's Lisa Su Seeks Expanded HBM Ties With Korean Chipmakers - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: AMD's Lisa Su Seeks Expanded HBM Ties With Korean Chipmakers  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su returned to South Korea seven months after her last visit and said the company will expand its high-bandwidth memory partnerships with Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS). AMD, a U.S. artificial intelligence chip company that develops central processing units and graphics processing units, also met Korean neural processing unit startups to discuss ways to showcase new computing infrastructure.
Su met Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, head of the Device Solutions division, and other senior executives at the company's Seocho office in Seoul on the 7th. After confirming in March this year the supply of HBM4 for AMD's next-generation AI accelerator, the Instinct MI455X, the two sides met again seven months later to discuss further cooperation extending into foundry, or contract chip manufacturing. Su also met SK hynix President Kwak Noh-jung to discuss ways to expand supply of HBM4 to be mounted on the MI455X.
With memory supply still falling short in the AI infrastructure market, Su expects the HBM partnerships to continue for an extended period. Speaking to reporters after AMD's Gamer Day event at Dragon City in Seoul's Yongsan district, she said the chip supply chain is highly complex, making it important to hold close and in-depth discussions with key partners such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. She said the company values relationships that run three to five years or longer over the medium to long term, rather than partnerships of one to three years. Su added that chipmaking is a team sport and that meeting partners frequently and regularly matters.
Beyond strengthening its memory supply chain in Korea, AMD plans to build a new NPU supply chain as well. To that end, Su met chief executives of Korean AI companies at the Four Seasons Hotel in Seoul's Jongno district on the same day to discuss specific areas of cooperation. A total of 13 companies attended the meeting, including domestic NPU developers such as FuriosaAI and DeepX as well as AI infrastructure solution providers such as MangoBoost. Su said AMD's principle has always been collaboration with an open ecosystem, and that AMD will create new opportunities for cooperation with leading Korean companies as the country builds up its competitiveness in AI. Participants discussed ways to link AMD's CPUs and GPUs with Korean-made AI chips, as well as participation in open-source AI and the ROCm high-performance computing software platform ecosystem.
The government plans to run a demonstration project for heterogeneous computing infrastructure built jointly by AMD and Korea's AI industry, and to develop it into a reference model that can be used in overseas markets. Ryu Je-myung, second vice minister of science and ICT, proposed partnerships across the government's three mega-projects covering semiconductors, AI data centers and physical AI, and Su described the plan as exactly the right direction and an ambitious vision while expressing willingness to take part, according to officials. AMD plans to establish an AI center of excellence in Korea this year and hire several hundred researchers.
Su's return after only seven months is seen as a sign of Korea's growing importance in the global AI market. With the arrival of AI agents sharply increasing demand for inference computing, officials say it is becoming more important to combine various computing resources based on cost and power efficiency rather than relying on GPUs alone. Lee Do-gyu, head of the information and communications policy office at the Ministry of Science and ICT, said AI infrastructure has developed around GPUs, but that as computing demand grows and the inference market expands, raising performance per watt and cost efficiency has become critical. The global question now is how to optimize CPUs, GPUs and NPUs to deliver the best performance at the lowest cost, Lee said.
Korea's solid manufacturing base is also drawing attention as a hub for physical AI, given the large number of manufacturers that can apply AI to actual products and factories. Su proposed "world models" used in physical AI as a field for joint research at the planned AI research center in Korea. AMD recently announced it would acquire World Labs, co-founded by Stanford University professor Fei-Fei Li, known as a godmother of AI, as it seeks to expand into physical AI.

articles.title: Taiwan and North Korea: two sides of the same coin – the Indo-Pacific - Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.summary: Taiwan and North Korea: two sides of the same coin – the Indo-Pacific  Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.full_text:
For decades, Washington and Beijing have dealt with the nuclear issue in Pyongyang and the Taiwan Strait issue separately. The two issues have now become intertwined, with consequences that extend as far as Europe and will test Italy’s position in the Indo-Pacific
For over thirty years, the West has regarded the North Korean nuclear issue as an issue separate from the other crises in East Asia. The idea was that the nuclear proliferation of Pyongyang could be addressed through disarmament negotiations and multilateral mechanisms, without linking it directly to the dispute over the future of Taiwan. However, developments in recent years have called this approach into question. The growing confrontation between the United States and China, together with the paralysis of the UN Security Council, has made it increasingly difficult to keep the two issues separate.
Beijing’s stance on North Korea’s nuclear and missile programme also depends on how the Chinese leadership perceives US moves regarding Taiwan. The issue of the Strait is a top priority for the People’s Republic, which regards the island as part of its territory and rejects any prospect of formal independence. The Americans, on the other hand, are committed to preserving peace and stability in the region.
Things are changing on the Korean Peninsula. For the US, the arsenal poses a direct threat to its own security and that of its allies. Meanwhile, Beijing keeps a watchful eye on the supreme leader Kim Jong-un, who acts as a buffer along the border with China. This has shaped relations between China and the United States regarding North Korea for years. Beijing has exerted pressure on Pyongyang, particularly when it has secured, in return, American guarantees on the Taiwan issue.
The Taiwan issue
The history of recent decades shows just how closely this balance has been linked to the situation in the Strait. During the first nuclear crisis of the 1990s, this link did not fully develop, partly due to the time lag between the Geneva Agreements and the subsequent Taiwan missile crisis (1995–1996). Between 2002 and 2008, during the Six-Party Talks – which included North Korea (the country at the centre of the crisis), South Korea, China, the United States, Russia and Japan – China played a central role in the negotiations with North Korea. At the time, the tensions caused by the initiatives of Chen Shui-bian administration in Taiwan prompted Beijing to exert pressure on Pyongyang, including in the energy and financial spheres; in return, China secured a commitment from Washington to preserve the status quo in the Strait.
This balance remained largely intact even during Ma Ying-jeou’s presidency in Taiwan, from 2008 to 2016. The easing of tensions over the issue of independence enabled Beijing to support and impose tougher sanctions against North Korea, including severe restrictions on coal imports and the freezing of certain financial channels used by Pyongyang.

[Yongin=Sports Chosun Kim Ga-eul Reporter] The South Korean national football team’s final home match of 2026 has concluded. South Korea wrapped up all home matches scheduled for this year with the game against Uzbekistan held at Yongin Mirae Stadium on October 6. The November A-matches are planned to be held away.
South Korean football faced constant criticism and slander throughout the year. Ultimately, following the group-stage exit at the 2026 North America World Cup, Chung Mong-gyu, head of the Korea Football Association (KFA), and coach Hong Myung-bo resigned. Subsequently, political circles demanded a restructuring. The government-led K-Football Innovation Committee was launched to fundamentally improve the structure of South Korean football. Amid the chaos, football had to continue, so the KFA’s National Team Strengthening Committee appointed Robert Moreno as interim coach.
Fans expected a fresh start, but reality was harsh. South Korea suffered a 1-4 defeat to Uruguay and managed only a 0-0 draw against Venezuela after a historically poor performance. The Taegeuk Warriors could not hide their dismay. Defensive key player Kim Min-jae, Bayern Munich, was substituted and left for the bench, showing a sharp reaction to Moreno. He eventually made a pointed remark: “Rather than individuals shining, the team must unite to achieve results. To elevate the team’s level, all players must ‘put their heads down’ and work hard.”
Players who should have freely roamed the field were only anxious. Midfield leader Hwang In-beom, Porto, said after the Venezuela match: “My body and mind are both tired. I’ve been in the national team for about nine years, but since then, many things in football and beyond needed change, yet they haven’t improved. I feel a lot of responsibility because I want South Korean football to develop. There’s no one to help. The KFA president is absent, and with an interim coach, we don’t know the future. As players, it’s not easy. I have many doubts about who can help. There are clear problems, but no one is stepping up, and there’s no one to take charge.” Eventually, retirement rumors about 1996-born peers Kim Min-jae, Hwang In-beom, and Hwang Hee-chan (Schalke) surfaced. Ace Lee Kang-in, Atlético Madrid, cautiously shared his thoughts: “It was a World Cup year. It was a difficult year. I don’t know what the future holds, but the past is the past. I should focus on how to perform better and build a competitive team.”
South Korean football is preparing for the 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia next January. However, the coach’s future remains uncertain. Moreno is scheduled to lead six A-matches from September to November. Depending on his evaluation, he could continue. But there is no decision-maker to finalize the situation. A KFA source said, “We cannot confirm the election schedule for the KFA president.” This election differs in scale: the number of voters will increase over 100 times to 20,000 people from the previous 192 in the 2025 election. Practical issues like electronic voting methods remain unresolved.
The Taegeuk Warriors’ tearful sighs are destined to repeat in this bleak present.

South Korea's household debt as a share of nominal gross domestic product fell to its lowest level in a decade at the end of the second quarter. While household debt continued to grow in absolute terms, nominal GDP expanded faster on the back of a semiconductor boom. Surplus funds held by companies also reached a record high.
The household debt-to-GDP ratio stood at 81.1% at the end of the second quarter, according to flow of funds data for the second quarter of 2026 released by the Bank of Korea on the 7th. That is down 4.2 percentage points from 85.3% in the previous quarter and the lowest since the second quarter of 2016, when the ratio was 80.2%.
The government has set a target of lowering the ratio to around 80% by 2030, meaning it has come close to that goal four years ahead of schedule.
Net lending by households and nonprofit organizations — funds invested minus funds raised — totaled 60.7 trillion won in the second quarter, down 18.5 trillion won from 79.2 trillion won in the previous quarter. Net lending refers to money flowing into financial assets minus debt, representing the increase in surplus funds held by an economic sector. When debt exceeds inflows, the sector becomes a net borrower. The BOK said surplus funds shrank as incomes fell and net home purchases rose.
Excluding funds raised, households invested 88.5 trillion won in the second quarter, down 7.8 trillion won from 96.3 trillion won in the previous quarter. Investment in equities and investment funds rose sharply to 101.6 trillion won from 61.4 trillion won, but deposits at financial institutions swung to minus 23.3 trillion won from 29.4 trillion won, reducing the overall total.
Net lending by nonfinancial corporations surged, driven by a jump in net profit led by semiconductor companies. It more than tripled to 67.1 trillion won in the second quarter from 20.8 trillion won in the first quarter, the highest since the data series began in 2009.
"Net profit at listed companies rose to 189 trillion won in the second quarter from 111 trillion won in the first quarter, helped by chipmakers, which expanded corporate net lending," said Kim Yong-hyun, head of the BOK's flow of funds team. "Companies increased their financial activity with the surge in surplus funds."

Bank of Japan FAQs
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

articles.title: Lisa Su Flew to Seoul Twice in Seven Months; AMD’s AI Roadmap Depends on Korea - Tech Times
articles.summary: Lisa Su Flew to Seoul Twice in Seven Months; AMD’s AI Roadmap Depends on Korea  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su landed in Seoul on Wednesday for her second visit to South Korea in seven months, spending the day in back-to-back meetings with the leaders of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix — the two companies that collectively control more than 80 percent of global high-bandwidth memory revenue, and whose allocation decisions will determine when, and in what quantities, AMD's Helios rack-scale AI systems ship. According to AMD's official announcement, the visit included AMD Gamer Day 2026 at Yongsan Dragon City and a media Q&A session the same afternoon.
The visit is AMD's most concentrated supply chain diplomacy of 2026, and it is happening at the CEO level — not with procurement teams — because the constraint AMD faces is not silicon. It is memory. Specifically, it is high-bandwidth memory: a category of chip that AMD itself invented, that only three companies in the world manufacture at meaningful scale, and that every single Helios AI rack requires in quantities of 31 terabytes per system. Getting to that number means AMD needs 432 gigabytes of HBM4 per GPU — 50 percent more than the 288 GB found in Nvidia's competing Vera Rubin GPU — and 72 such GPUs per rack, making HBM supply the most consequential variable in AMD's ability to deliver on its data center commitments.
Su met with Jun Young-hyun, Vice Chairman and CEO of Samsung's Device Solutions division, in Samsung's Seocho office in Gangnam, and separately with SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung — meetings that continue the roadmap discussions opened by the March MOU and push them toward the three-to-five-year planning horizons Su has described publicly. "We have gotten great support from both Samsung and SK Hynix, and we view the partnerships on HBM not just one generation but really multiple generations," Su told reporters at a media briefing in Seoul on Wednesday, citing planning horizons of three to five years or more. "To build a solid supply chain over the long term, it is important to work closely with our partners."
What High-Bandwidth Memory Is, and Why It Made Seoul Indispensable
High-bandwidth memory did not arrive from a Korean laboratory. It was conceived at AMD in 2008, developed by a team led by AMD Senior Fellow Bryan Black, and brought to JEDEC standardization in 2013 through a proposal co-submitted by AMD and SK Hynix. The first HBM chip was manufactured by SK Hynix; the first product to ship with it was the AMD Radeon R9 Fury X GPU in 2015 — a history detailed in the Wikipedia HBM article. The technology solved a problem that was choking GPU performance: conventional memory interfaces were too narrow to feed chips with the compute throughput AI and graphics workloads demand.
The solution was architectural. Where conventional DRAM connects to a processor over a narrow bus — GDDR6 uses 32-bit channels — HBM stacks multiple DRAM dies vertically and connects them to the GPU through a silicon interposer using through-silicon vias (TSVs) and microbumps, creating a bus up to 2,048 bits wide in the current HBM4 generation. That wide interface means the memory can run at more moderate clock speeds while still delivering bandwidth that dwarfs what conventional DRAM can provide. The MI455X carries 12 HBM4 stacks of 36 GB each, connected over that 2,048-bit interface, producing 23.3 terabytes per second of peak memory bandwidth per GPU. For comparison, HBM3E — the prior generation now shipping in AMD's MI350X and MI355X — uses a 1,024-bit interface and delivers roughly half that bandwidth per stack.
The manufacturing process for HBM stacks requires extraordinary precision. DRAM dies are thinned to roughly 30 micrometers — about a third the width of a human hair — stacked up to 16 layers high, and interconnected through TSVs. The finished stack then bonds to a silicon interposer fabricated by TSMC under its CoWoS-L (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate, Local interconnect) process. That interposer routes signals between the HBM stacks and the GPU compute dies on the same package. The practical consequence is that HBM4 supply involves two separate chokepoints: the Korean companies that produce the memory stacks themselves, and TSMC's advanced packaging capacity that assembles them with the GPU. Su's Seoul visit addresses the first of those chokepoints directly.
Because the DRAM stacking process requires specialized fabrication equipment and yields that have taken years to develop, high-volume HBM manufacturing remains concentrated in three companies — Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology — with Samsung and SK Hynix together accounting for the large majority of global output. AMD, the company that proposed the HBM standard and shipped the first HBM product, does not manufacture memory. It designs accelerators and depends entirely on partners to supply the chip at the heart of its most important product line.
What the March MOU Established, and What Wednesday's Meetings Extended
Su's first Korea visit, in March 2026, produced the most consequential supply agreement in AMD's recent history. On March 18, she signed a memorandum of understanding with Jun Young-hyun at Samsung's advanced manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Seoul. The Samsung-AMD HBM4 agreement formalized Samsung as AMD's primary HBM4 supplier for the Instinct MI455X — the first time Samsung had been elevated to primary HBM supplier status for an AMD GPU — and extended collaboration to DDR5 memory for AMD's 6th Generation EPYC "Venice" server processors. That evening, Samsung Chairman Lee Jae-yong hosted Su for dinner at Seungjiwon, the Samsung Group's historic guesthouse, where the two executives discussed deepening the partnership across multiple semiconductor categories including, potentially, foundry services.
The March agreement was urgent in part because of competitive dynamics that had already squeezed AMD's HBM4 access. SK Hynix, which commands approximately 54 to 58 percent of global HBM revenue, had already committed the large majority of its 2026 HBM4 capacity — estimates put the figure at roughly 70 percent — to Nvidia for the Vera Rubin platform. That concentration left AMD with limited access to SK Hynix supply for next-generation products and drove the strategic pivot toward Samsung as the primary memory anchor. With Samsung's HBM4 achieving what the company described as an "80 percent golden yield" by mid-2026 and the company's share of HBM4 shipments rising as SK Hynix encountered validation delays in Q2 2026, the March MOU has taken on additional strategic weight.
Wednesday's meetings represent a continuation of the roadmap work that the March MOU opened. Su has described these conversations in terms that go well beyond any individual purchase order, citing planning horizons of three to five years or more and positioning both companies as co-suppliers rather than alternatives — a supply chain strategy that reduces AMD's exposure to single-source risk on the memory that now defines its most important product line.
What Is Riding on Helios
The urgency of Su's second Korea visit in seven months becomes concrete when measured against what AMD has committed to deliver. At the Advancing AI 2026 conference in San Francisco in July, AMD formally launched the Helios rack-scale platform alongside the Instinct MI455X accelerator. A Helios rack integrates 72 MI455X GPUs with 18 6th-generation EPYC Venice processors, per AMD's Helios rack specifications, along with AMD's Pensando networking hardware, and a liquid cooling infrastructure, all unified through a 31 TB pool of shared HBM4 memory connected via AMD's UALink (Ultra Accelerator Link) scale-up fabric — an open alternative to Nvidia's proprietary NVLink interconnect. AMD has claimed the system outperforms Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 by 15 percent on FP4 compute performance, with 50 percent greater memory capacity and scale-out bandwidth; those claims, based on AMD's internal benchmarks, have not been independently replicated by neutral parties as of October 2026.
Su made the memory dependency explicit at the July launch. "Help from SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics is what made the next-generation MI455 and Helios possible as we developed them," she said. That acknowledgment is not a courtesy; it is an operational reality. AMD's September 2026 appearance at Citi's Global TMT Conference produced a candid acknowledgment that the company is actively managing supply constraints: "We need to expand supply, but the supply of components such as HBM and semiconductor substrates is very tight, and there are also constraints on advanced packaging capacity," an AMD executive stated at the event, per Korea Herald reporting. That packaging constraint refers to TSMC's CoWoS-L capacity, which serves as the second supply chain bottleneck independent of how much HBM4 Samsung and SK Hynix can produce.
At AMD's second-quarter 2026 earnings report in August, the company posted data center revenue of $6.7 billion — up 107 percent year over year and representing 58 percent of AMD's record $11.5 billion in total revenue. CFO Jean Hu stated that data center sales were expected to "accelerate in the second half of 2026, driving stronger overall revenue growth and continued earnings expansion," with Helios ramp cited as a key driver.
The SK Hynix Question
While Samsung is AMD's confirmed primary HBM4 partner, Wednesday's meeting between Su and Kwak Noh-jung carries its own strategic weight. SK Hynix has been so deeply integrated into Nvidia's supply chain that AMD's relationship with the company on cutting-edge HBM has been structurally limited. Analysts and Korean trade publications have been watching to see whether AMD and SK Hynix will move toward a more substantive HBM4 arrangement, particularly as demand from AMD, Google, Microsoft, Oracle, and other hyperscalers pushes total HBM requirements well beyond what Nvidia alone can absorb.

Since the steel industry accounts for about 15% of domestic greenhouse gas emissions, a key challenge is to shift from production centered on conventional blast furnaces to low-carbon processes.
POSCO Holdings President Lee Jutae said, "A hydrogen-reduction steelworks that operates around the clock needs stable and affordable clean energy. A green premium market must also be established, one that recognizes the environmental value of low-carbon steel in economic terms."

LG Electronics and Samsung Electronics are seeking to expand the heat pump market, which replaces fossil fuels with electricity for residential heating. Solar panels generate electricity, which is stored in an ESS and a thermal storage system and then used by home appliances, electric vehicles and heat pumps. A home energy management system integrates the management of energy production, storage and consumption.
LG Electronics plans to establish a domestic heat pump supply system based at its Changwon plant and expand to other local governments a demonstration project on the electrification of heating and cooling conducted at a multi-unit housing complex on Jeju Island. It will then develop energy-independent residential complexes in distributed energy special zones and youth housing in South Jeolla Province, before expanding the scope of application over the long term to public rental housing and private multi-unit residences.

After establishing design and installation standards suited to domestic climate conditions, it plans to conduct demonstrations in carbon-zero apartments and expand distribution to general housing and public buildings.

China will monitor the United Kingdom’s moves on tariffs targeting Chinese electric vehicles and respond accordingly, as London considers whether to introduce new trade measures against Chinese-made EVs. The issue has emerged amid growing concerns in Britain and other major economies over Chinese industrial capacity, government support and the competitive pressure facing domestic automakers.
Beijing’s position comes as the UK weighs possible tariffs on Chinese electric cars. British officials have been consulting industry representatives over potential measures, but the UK has not yet formally imposed a new China-specific tariff on electric vehicles. Any decision would therefore represent a shift in Britain’s current trade approach toward Chinese EV imports.
China has increasingly objected to what it regards as protectionist restrictions on its electric-vehicle exports. Its Commerce Ministry has previously said measures restricting Chinese EVs should comply with World Trade Organization rules and has opposed what it considers discriminatory trade barriers.
In January, China’s Commerce Ministry said Beijing and the European Union had made progress in consultations over the EU’s anti-subsidy case concerning Chinese battery-electric vehicles. The ministry said both sides had agreed that Chinese exporters could pursue price commitments as a way of addressing European concerns within the WTO framework.
China has also taken steps to regulate its own electric-vehicle exports. Since January 1, 2026, China has required export licences for pure-electric passenger vehicles, under rules introduced by the Commerce Ministry, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, General Administration of Customs and State Administration for Market Regulation. Beijing said the system was intended to promote the healthy development of new-energy vehicle trade and regulate export activity.
The UK’s position is complicated by its broader industrial policy. London has been reviewing its zero-emission vehicle strategy while seeking to support domestic manufacturing and investment. The government said in August that more than one in four new cars sold in Britain were electric and that EV sales had risen 45% year-on-year in July. articles.title: KOSPI Trapped Below 7,000: Foreign Exodus, Semiconductor Doubts - 조선일보
articles.summary: KOSPI Trapped Below 7,000: Foreign Exodus, Semiconductor Doubts  조선일보
articles.full_text:
While the U.S. New York stock market continues to set new all-time highs, the KOSPI remains stuck below the 7,000 level.
On the 6th (local time), the U.S. S&P 500 index closed at 7,818.95, up 0.58% from the previous trading day, while the Nasdaq index rose 0.45% to 27,599.79. Both indices hit new all-time highs. In contrast, the South Korean stock market is moving in the opposite direction. On the 7th, the KOSPI closed at 6,803.90, down 1.98% from the previous trading day. It has fallen 25% from its peak. While U.S. stock markets set new highs daily, why is the KOSPI struggling to break out of the 7,000 range?
◇Foreign Investors Have Left
The biggest difference lies in supply and demand. Global funds continue to flow into the U.S. stock market, particularly focusing on artificial intelligence (AI) companies. According to Reuters, U.S. equity funds saw a net inflow of 20.6 billion dollars (approximately 28 trillion Korean won) over the week ending on September 30. Of this, 19.3 billion dollars flowed into large-cap funds alone. The previous week saw an even larger net inflow of 37.49 billion dollars.
In contrast, foreign investors are exiting South Korea. According to the Korea Exchange, foreign investors net sold 21.5246 trillion Korean won worth of KOSPI stocks during September. They sold 4.8922 trillion Korean won worth of Samsung Electronics and 11.5844 trillion Korean won worth of SK Hynix. Foreign investors’ monthly net purchases of these two stocks turned to net selling starting from May. Kim Jae-seung, a researcher at Hyundai Motor Securities, analyzed, “The continued net selling by foreign investors has driven Samsung Electronics’ foreign ownership ratio to its lowest level in the past decade,” adding, “SK Hynix’s foreign ownership ratio has also reverted to levels seen before the AI bull market that began in 2023 following the release of ChatGPT-3.5.”
◇Doubts About Memory Chip Stock Prices
Within AI semiconductor companies, evaluations of memory and non-memory sectors are diverging. On the 6th, Nvidia rose 0.14%, approaching a market capitalization of 6 trillion dollars. Marvell Technology, a semiconductor design company, surged 5.81% on expectations that its Total Addressable Market (TAM) — the maximum revenue achievable by 2030 — would expand to 400 billion dollars. AMD also hit a record high after CEO Lisa Su stated, “The situation where demand exceeds supply will continue for several years.” However, memory companies Micron fell 1.73%, and SK Hynix’s American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) dropped 6.39% on the same day. On the 7th, in the domestic market, Samsung Electronics fell 1.29%, and SK Hynix declined 2.82%. Among AI semiconductors, only memory stocks are declining. U.S. investment magazine Barron’s reported, “Investors are questioning whether memory semiconductor stocks can continue to rise,” adding, “Analysts expect memory prices to peak around mid-2027.”
A new variable has emerged: power shortages at data centers. On the 5th, Morgan Stanley stated, “U.S. data center developers may fail to secure 34% of the power needed by 2028,” adding, “In such a scenario, while Nvidia and Broadcom would be relatively less affected, memory, optical component, and other secondary chip manufacturers could face impacts.” It noted that if data center construction is canceled, memory and optical component companies would be most vulnerable to inventory management issues.
Is there no possibility for the KOSPI to break out of the 7,000 range? The securities industry still leaves room for possibility. Han Ji-young, a researcher at Kiwoom Securities, said, “As concerns over U.S. market interest rates and rising oil prices are easing, the KOSPI’s resilience is unlikely to weaken further,” adding, “If Samsung Electronics’ third-quarter earnings are strong, we expect improvements in foreign investor demand.”

articles.title: Lisa Su: "Semiconductors Are a Team Sport"... Emphasizes Long-Term Cooperation with Samsung and SK - Inven Global

articles.full_text:
AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su praised South Korea as a vital market not only in terms of the memory supply chain, but also for its AI development ecosystem. She expressed her intent to expand long-term collaboration with Korean companies including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, while actively engaging with the AI ecosystem spanning startups and universities.
AMD hosted 'AMD GAMERS DAY' on the 7th at Dragon City in Yongsan, Seoul. Following the event, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su and Jack Huynh, Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Computing and Graphics Group, attended a media Q&A session.
During the Q&A, a wide array of topics was addressed, ranging from collaboration with South Korean semiconductor companies to AI data center demand, HBM4 and next-generation AI systems, the Korean startup ecosystem, personal AI, and expanding FSR across APUs.
Throughout the Q&A, CEO Lisa Su repeatedly emphasized that "Korea is a crucial market for AMD in terms of both supply chain and partnerships." She explained that given the rapid increase in AI demand, companies must plan their supply chains together looking ahead three to five years, rather than just one or two years.
Q. Cooperation between AMD and South Korean companies, including Samsung Electronics, is expanding. How do you view the Korean supply chain?
Lisa Su: Korea has many great partners. Samsung, in particular, is one of AMD's most strategic partners across multiple technology areas, including memory.
In today's semiconductor industry, working closely with partners to plan long-term supply chains is extremely important. Demand in the AI sector is very high, and strong demand continues in the gaming and consumer markets as well. In that regard, collaborating closely with South Korean partners such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is crucial.
Ultimately, I believe semiconductors are a 'team sport.' It requires many partners working together, and AMD regularly meets and communicates with key partners. AI is moving faster than any field I have experienced so far, so the more we communicate with partners, the better we can respond to market demand.
Q. How would you rate South Korea's AI startup and development ecosystem? What plans does AMD hope to pursue in Korea?
Lisa Su: What makes Korea special is the wealth of talent across various fields—from the supply chain to universities, startups, and major conglomerates.
AMD is heavily focused on AI right now. AI is one of the fastest-growing areas of AMD's business and is being rapidly adopted worldwide. Korea has many innovative startups in both hardware and software.
This morning, I met with government officials and several startups, and I was impressed by the culture of actively seeking new approaches. Beyond companies like Upstage that work closely with AMD, I met with various startups eager to join AMD's open ecosystem.
AMD plans to actively work toward establishing an AI 'Center of Excellence' in Korea while expanding collaboration with startups and universities. I believe Korea is a fantastic place to drive AI development.
Q. How do you view current demand in the data center market, including next-generation AI products? What is demand like specifically in the Korean market?
Lisa Su: Demand across data centers is extremely strong. In Korea as well, we continuously hear calls for more AI hardware and expanded AI computing capabilities.
The Korean supply chain is vital for AMD to achieve these goals. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are core partners and will play a critical role as we fulfill our objectives in data centers and AI. We see the current demand environment as very robust.
Q. With rising AI demand, memory supply is tight and cost burdens are growing. How is AMD responding?
Lisa Su: Memory is an essential component of the overall computing system. It is true that the current supply environment is quite tight.
AMD has built deep partnerships across the memory supply chain, which has also helped significantly grow our business recently. At the same time, we continue to look for ways to utilize memory more efficiently.
We are working with customers to optimize memory usage in each system so that more computing can be processed with the same resources. We are also asking our supply partners to expand production capacity as quickly as possible.
AMD itself has grown significantly over the past few years. Therefore, securing a broad foundation in the supply chain is essential, and we are continuing to explore new possibilities for collaboration with Samsung in various areas.
Q. Is your return visit to Korea this year due to the memory shortage, or did you have broader collaboration in mind?
Lisa Su: I wish I could visit Korea more often. The main reason for visiting Korea again this time is that Korea's ecosystem is immensely important to AMD, both on the supply side and in terms of partnerships.
In an environment like this, we cannot simply plan for the next one or two years with our partners. Because supply chains are so complex, we must look ahead three to five years and plan together.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are highly critical partners in that regard. At the same time, Korea has many innovative companies. AMD wants to build a broader foundation in Korea and support the local ecosystem.
Q. I understand that a $10 billion collaboration plan was recently announced in Taiwan. Can we expect a similar scale of cooperation in South Korea?
Lisa Su: The semiconductor supply chain does not consist of memory alone. It encompasses wafers, packaging, memory, and various components that make up a system. Therefore, the supply chain must be built globally, and each area must collaborate.
Yesterday, I met with various customers and partners in Taiwan, and today I met with our partners in Korea. AMD will make investments worth tens of billions of dollars across the global supply chain.
The scale of business between South Korea and AMD is also substantial. In particular, I believe there are many areas across the supply chain, including memory, where we can work together.
Q. As demand for AI computing grows, both AMD and its competitors are strengthening cooperation with Korean memory makers. Do you see the competition for memory supply as a risk factor?
Lisa Su: What matters most in the market right now is that demand for AI computing continues to rise. Every company in the supply chain is moving quickly to meet that demand.
From AMD's perspective, how early and how deeply we share our plans with partners is what matters. The more we plan together, the better we can satisfy end-user demand.
The semiconductor industry is in a very dynamic period right now. Our goal is to meet as much demand as possible, and as demand continues to surge, we are considering every option to expand supply.
Q. How far along are the preparations for next-generation products using HBM4 from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix?
Lisa Su: We have already begun shipments of our next-generation MI455X and AMD Helios solutions. These systems utilize HBM4, and we are receiving tremendous support from both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
We view our HBM collaboration not merely as a single-generation effort, but as a partnership that spans multiple generations.
You might not know this, but AMD has been incorporating HBM into actual products since 2015. We have accumulated long-standing experience in integrating high-bandwidth memory and complex technology into a single system. We are currently very satisfied with the results of HBM4, and we are expanding production and deployment scale.
Q. For Senior Vice President Jack Huynh: You mentioned expanding FSR to APUs and handhelds. Will this support existing APUs, or do you plan to release new processors?
Jack Huynh: We intend to do both. Because AMD values gaming and gamers deeply, we plan to expand FSR technology across APUs.
We aren't simply expanding the reach of existing technology, either. We have also built a lighter new model tailored for APU environments. The goal is to provide solid visuals and low latency even in constrained hardware environments.
We plan to expand this across our APU lineup within this year, and you will see it in a variety of products, including gaming laptops. We will make further announcements on the details within the year.
Q. What are your impressions of Korea's AI technology, and how do you view the growth potential of personal AI?
Jack Huynh: The pace of technological advancement in South Korea is remarkably fast and impressive. At AMD, we see immense potential in personal AI and distributed AI.
While AI models can be trained in the cloud, the efficiency of open-weight models has been increasing at a rapid pace recently. Workloads of a scale that were difficult to run locally just a year ago can now be executed on increasingly smaller systems, and the innovation cycle is accelerating from six months down to three or even two months.
As a result, substantial AI workloads can now be processed locally. Local processing offers distinct advantages in privacy and security, while also reducing cloud operational costs.
That doesn't mean everything should be processed locally. We believe the best approach is to handle suitable tasks locally, and leverage the cloud when greater computing power is required. AMD envisions a direction that utilizes every available computing resource, from the cloud to the edge and the client.

articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- USD/JPY traded near 158.35 in early Asian dealings, supported by softer Bank of Japan rate hike expectations.
- Overnight index swaps showed current odds of a BoJ rate increase this month around 12%, down from 40% early last week, while probabilities approached 90% when December is included.
- September US Nonfarm Payrolls rose by 29K versus a 90K consensus, prompting traders to trim expectations for a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike.
BoJ Caution Undermines Yen, Focus Turns to Fed Minutes
USD/JPY stayed supported around 158.35 during early Asian trading on Wednesday, as diminishing prospects for an imminent Bank of Japan (BoJ) rate hike pressured the Japanese Yen against the US Dollar. Market participants are now looking to the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) Minutes due later on Wednesday for further guidance on US monetary policy.
BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda stated on Tuesday that the central bank would “assess the likelihood and risks of the baseline economic and price outlook being realized” when considering the pace and timing of further rate increases. This has reinforced expectations that policymakers will adopt a measured approach at the October monetary policy meeting, limiting support for the Yen.
Separately, Reuters reported on Tuesday that new BoJ policymaker Ayano Sato backs lifting interest rates in multiple stages. Even so, market-derived pricing signals little urgency for the next move.
Market Pricing Shows Lower Near-Term BoJ Hike Odds
Overnight index swaps indicated that investors currently assign about a 12% probability to a BoJ rate hike this month, a notable decline from levels as high as 40% early last week, according to Bloomberg. When the December meeting is factored in, the implied likelihood of a hike rises to around 90%.

Soft US Labor Data Eases Fed Hike Expectations
On the US side, weaker labor market figures have led traders to scale back expectations for a Federal Reserve rate increase this month. Data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Friday showed that Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) increased by 29K in September, versus a 133K gain in August and below market forecasts of 90K. The Unemployment Rate edged up to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
Rabobank: Gradual BoJ Path, Elevated USD/JPY, Intervention Fears
Analysts at Rabobank highlighted that, following the “as expected 25 bps rate rise last month,” market pricing now “suggests only a limited prospect of a policy move at the October 30 meeting, with expectations centring on December for the next policy move.” While BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated that policymakers intend to “continue raising the policy interest rate” and characterized the Japanese economy as expanding “moderately,” Rabobank believes “this strengthens the market’s expectation that back-to-back rate hikes BoJ are unlikely.” As they further noted, “even so, the Bank is still not widely viewed as being in a position in which back-to-back rate rises are appropriate,” although “this may suggest that a hastened pace of rate hikes is possible, though clearly that depends on how the economy develops in the months ahead.”
Externally, Rabobank’s base case is that “the market has anticipated too much Fed policy tightening next year.” They argue that, “assuming some Fed rate hike risk is priced out, USD/JPY has the potential to move lower into 2027,” but currently “we maintain a 3-month USD/JPY target of 155.00.” Although USD/JPY has climbed since the September policy decision, Rabobank observes that “the market is fearful that a return to levels close to 160, could again trigger further intervention.” In their view, the BoJ’s inflation goal “now appears to have reached the point when it can instead shift its focus to stabilising price pressures around the target level,” bolstering expectations of a gradual, rather than forceful, tightening cycle.
Fed’s Schmid Strikes Hawkish Tone, AI Cited as Inflation Driver
Fed’s Schmid delivered a notably hawkish message, earning an 8/10 score on the FXS Speechtracker, slightly higher than the 7.5/10 historical average and pointing to a firmer-than-usual policy stance. Emphasizing that inflation is “frustrating,” that the Fed “still has a way to go,” and that AI is now “one of the largest drivers of inflation,” the remarks underscored worries about persistent price pressures and new structural forces. The warning that Fed credibility is on the line and that “the Fed still has work to do on the short rate despite higher long-term yields” signaled tolerance for maintaining or even tightening policy in the face of elevated bond yields.
The FXS Fed Sentiment Index increased by 0.34 points to 137.91, indicating that the broader tone of Fed communication remains firmly hawkish and well above the neutral 100 level. This modest rise, in line with the stronger speech score, suggests that Fed messaging continues to underpin a resilient Dollar bias as markets price in a sustained period of restrictive monetary policy.

articles.title: Samsung reaches new profit record with memory chip windfall - The Business Times
articles.summary: Samsung reaches new profit record with memory chip windfall  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Operating profit climbs to 107.4 trillion won, lifted by high-bandwidth memory demand
[SEOUL] Samsung Electronics posted another record profit that was just shy of sky-high expectations elevated by surging memory chip prices and relentless spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The company’s operating profit for the three months through September climbed to about 107.4 trillion won (US$80.1 billion), more than eight times the level a year earlier, lifted by demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.
That was still about 1 per cent short of the average of analysts’ forecasts of 108.7 trillion won, as the South Korean chips-to-smartphones conglomerate grapples with tighter margins in consumer electronics due to higher component prices.
Revenue came to 195 trillion won, also lower than expectations, preliminary numbers showed on Thursday (Oct 8).
“These are solid numbers,” said Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research.
“They’ve got a lot up their sleeve for next year with HBM, mostly because the full effect hasn’t even landed yet.”
The record numbers and high expectations underscore how sharply the economics of the AI boom have swung in favour of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology, as data centre developers race to secure memory chips for their AI servers.
Counterpoint Research raised its forecast for third-quarter DRAM prices to a 10 to 20 per cent sequential increase, from 5 to 10 per cent previously, saying customers are pulling forward orders alongside gains in pricing power among suppliers.
AI boom cycle
The boom has transformed Samsung’s semiconductor business, which only a few years ago was grappling with losses after a punishing downturn in demand.
Now, the AI infrastructure buildout is absorbing vast amounts of advanced DRAM, while Samsung is gaining ground on SK Hynix in HBM, the critical chips used alongside Nvidia and other AI accelerators.
The strength of the cycle is also showing up in South Korea’s trade data, with semiconductor exports more than tripling from September 2025.
Analysts on average estimate Samsung’s chip division will post an operating profit of 110 trillion won while its electronics unit will report a loss.
The Suwon-based company will release its full financial statement on Oct 29.
Samsung’s shares remain about 25 per cent below their June peak even after the company reported record-breaking results in July.
Investors retain a measure of skepticism around soaring profits in a sector prone to boom-and-bust cycles.
Samsung and SK Hynix are now expanding production capacity while also increasingly backing companies in the AI sector in a bid to drive more demand for their products. BLOOMBERG
